questions.q: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride (CH₃COCl) with dimethylcadmium ((CH₃)₂Cd) to give a ketone. Name the ketone product.
questions.a: CH₃COCl + (CH₃)₂Cd → CH₃COCH₃ (propanone/acetone) + CdCl₂. A wrong answer (e.g., using RMgX instead of R₂Cd, or writing a tertiary alcohol product) reveals the student does not understand that Grignard reagents over-add to acyl chlorides, while dialkylcadmium stops at the ketone due to lower reactivity.

questions.q: Explain why a Grignard reagent (RMgX) cannot be used directly on an acyl chloride to prepare a ketone, but works on a nitrile to give a ketone after hydrolysis.
questions.a: Grignard reagents are highly reactive and add twice to acyl chlorides: first to give a ketone, which is more reactive than the acyl chloride, so a second addition occurs yielding a tertiary alkoxide (→ tertiary alcohol after hydrolysis). With nitriles, the first addition gives an imine anion (C=N⁻MgX⁺) which is less electrophilic than a carbonyl, so a second addition is slow; hydrolysis of the imine yields the ketone. A wrong answer (e.g., "Grignard is not strong enough") shows confusion about relative electrophilicity and reaction stoichiometry.

questions.q: Predict the ketone product when butanenitrile (CH₃CH₂CH₂CN) reacts with phenylmagnesium bromide (PhMgBr) followed by dilute H₃O⁺. Write the stepwise equations.
questions.a: Step 1: CH₃CH₂CH₂CN + PhMgBr → CH₃CH₂CH₂C(=NMgBr)Ph (imine salt). Step 2: Hydrolysis: CH₃CH₂CH₂C(=NMgBr)Ph + H₂O/H⁺ → CH₃CH₂CH₂COPh (1-phenylpentan-1-one) + NH₄⁺ + MgBr(OH). A wrong product (e.g., forgetting the phenyl group, or writing an alcohol) indicates failure to track the R group from the Grignard reagent and/or misunderstanding that hydrolysis of an imine gives a carbonyl, not an alcohol.

questions.q: Compare the reactivity of acyl chlorides and nitriles toward Grignard reagents. Why does the nitrile route require an explicit hydrolysis step while the acyl chloride route with dialkylcadmium does not?
questions.a: Acyl chlorides are highly electrophilic; even the less reactive dialkylcadmium adds once to give a ketone directly (the CdCl₂ byproduct precipitates). Nitriles are less electrophilic; Grignard adds once to give a stable imine salt that must be hydrolyzed to reveal the ketone. A wrong comparison (e.g., "nitriles are more reactive") reveals a misunderstanding of carbonyl vs. cyano electrophilicity and the role of the leaving group (Cl⁻ vs. N⁻).

questions.q: A student attempts to prepare 2-phenylpropan-1-one (PhCOCH₂CH₃) by reacting propanoyl chloride (CH₃CH₂COCl) with phenylmagnesium bromide. Evaluate this plan and suggest the correct reagent.
questions.a: The plan fails: PhMgBr will add twice to propanoyl chloride, giving Ph₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃ (a tertiary alcohol) after hydrolysis. The correct reagent is diphenylcadmium ((Ph)₂Cd), prepared from CdCl₂ and 2 PhMgBr. A student who says "it will work" or suggests using only 1 equivalent of Grignard shows they do not grasp that ketone intermediates are more reactive than acyl chlorides toward Grignard reagents, making stoichiometric control impossible.

questions.q: Design a two-step synthesis of 4-methylpentan-2-one (CH₃COCH₂CH(CH₃)₂) starting from an acyl chloride and a suitable organometallic reagent. Specify all reagents and conditions.
questions.a: Target ketone: CH₃COCH₂CH(CH₃)₂. Disconnect at the carbonyl: acyl chloride = CH₃COCl (ethanoyl chloride); organometallic = (CH₂CH(CH₃)₂)₂Cd (di(3-methylbutyl)cadmium). Step 1: Prepare Grignard: (CH₃)₂CHCH₂MgBr from (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Br + Mg/ether. Step 2: 2 (CH₃)₂CHCH₂MgBr + CdCl₂ → ((CH₃)₂CHCH₂)₂Cd + 2 MgBrCl. Step 3: CH₃COCl + ((CH₃)₂CHCH₂)₂Cd → CH₃COCH₂CH(CH₃)₂ + CdCl₂. A poor answer (wrong carbon count, wrong reagent) reveals inability to perform retrosynthetic disconnection at the carbonyl.
